summary: An experimental document that compares the functionality of LPD and IPP and helps with building gateways between the two protocols. It is part of the set of documents describing IPP.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2569 explains how a gateway can translate between the LPD and IPP printing protocols. It also identifies features that cannot be mapped and warns that future IPP versions may differ.

questions: what is the difference between lpd and ipp
how to map lpd commands to ipp operations
what is an lpd to ipp mapper
which lpd functions have no ipp equivalent
subtitle: How a gateway can translate print jobs and requests between LPD and IPP.

tldr.problem: LPD and IPP use different commands, attributes, and job models, so gateway implementers need a defined way to translate between them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps LPD commands and control-file functions to IPP operations and attributes, and describes the reverse mapping and queue-status response formats.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document, not an Internet standard. Its IESG note warns that a future standards-track IPP version was expected to change.

today: RFC 2569 is an Experimental RFC published in April 1999. Its IESG note says it is not on the standards track and warns that a future standards-track version was expected to differ.

sections.title: Why the Protocols Need a Mapping
sections.content:
RFC 2569 helps implementers build gateways between the Line Printer Daemon (LPD) protocol and Internet Printing Protocol (IPP/1.0). It maps in both directions and compares the functions of the two protocols.

The mapping reflects existing LPD practice described by RFC 1179 and does not cover vendor extensions. The memo is an experimental example and is not on the standards track.
sections.plainLanguage: LPD and IPP express print jobs differently. A gateway uses the mappings in this RFC to translate requests and job details between them.

sections.title: LPD Commands to IPP Operations
sections.content:
The LPD-to-IPP mapper ignores print-any-waiting-jobs, because an IPP printer handles queued jobs without that command. It maps remove-jobs to Cancel-Job and queue-status requests to Get-Printer-Attributes and Get-Jobs.

An LPD job with one data file can map to Print-Job. For multiple files, the mapper uses Create-Job and Send-Document when supported; otherwise each file becomes a separate IPP job. The mapper rejects a data file whose byte count is zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway converts each LPD command into an IPP operation or set of operations. Some commands are unnecessary for IPP, and some multi-file jobs may become separate jobs.

sections.title: Queue Listings and Job Attributes
sections.content:
RFC 1179 does not define the format of queue-status replies, so RFC 2569 specifies short and long forms. The short form lists printer status, a heading, and one line per job; the long form gives each job a block with descriptions and file lines.

The mapper derives fields from IPP attributes such as job ID, document name, job size, and copies. The short form truncates the file-name list to 24 characters. LPD control-file functions provide job and document attributes such as the requesting user, job name, and document format.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines two queue-list formats and explains which IPP attributes supply their fields. Some LPD job details have no matching IPP feature.

sections.title: IPP Operations to LPD Commands
sections.content:
The reverse mapper translates IPP print operations into LPD job-receive commands and queue-reading operations into LPD queue-status commands. It handles Validate-Job itself because LPD supports few attributes.

The mapper creates LPD control-file lines in a specified order. LPD supports only a limited set of job information, so some requested IPP attributes cannot be reported back. The RFC does not define error-code conversion.
sections.plainLanguage: The reverse mapping packages IPP requests into the commands and control-file lines LPD expects. LPD can report only a limited set of job and printer details.

sections.title: Security and Unsupported Functions
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no security issues beyond those in the IPP model and transport documents and the LPD document. An IESG note expects a later standards-track protocol to add strong authentication and privacy features and warns that future versions might not interoperate with this one.

Appendix C lists LPD functions with no IPP equivalent. Some are ignored; unsupported document formats can cause a job to be rejected unless the format is registered.
sections.plainLanguage: The mapping does not add a separate security mechanism. The RFC warns that later standards-track versions may change the protocol and that some LPD functions have no IPP equivalent.
